claims.text: The starting AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are nearly equiatomic.
The starting nanoparticles have a homogeneous atomic arrangement at room temperature.
Controlled heating to near 1000°C will preserve the homogeneous atomic distribution until a critical temperature is reached.
Above the critical temperature, chemical segregation or phase transformations will become detectable.
In situ aberration-corrected STEM combined with EELS can investigate the thermal behavior of these nanoparticles at atomic resolution.
Atomic-resolution STEM imaging can track atomic configuration and displacement during heating.
EELS spectra can monitor changes in chemical composition or segregation during heating.
Enhanced thermodynamic contributions in high-entropy systems stabilize the multimetal distribution.
The proposed thermodynamic stabilization prevents atomic-scale structural change until thermal energy overcomes it.
Overcoming the proposed stabilization produces observable structural changes.
Below the critical temperature, STEM and EELS will show minimal atomic displacement or chemical segregation.
Above the critical temperature, slight phase segregation or minor atomic rearrangements will become evident.
Existing theoretical predictions and computational models suggest enhanced stability in high-entropy alloys.
Direct atomic-scale experimental evidence for the proposed enhanced stability is absent.
Changing the heating rate or environmental conditions may alter the observed behavior.
Measurement artifacts or differences in nanoparticle preparation could influence the observed effects.
